data.title: Alexander Ruttkay: On Svatopluk and Nitra – an archaeologist’s reflection
data.excerpt: An essay by the archaeologist Alexander Ruttkay on Svatopluk I, his bond with Nitra and what the 9th century means for Slovak historical awareness. Published with the author’s permission; it appeared in Literárny týždenník and on the page of the Klub priateľov starej Nitry (Club of Friends of Old Nitra).
data.metaTitle: Alexander Ruttkay: On Svatopluk and Nitra
data.metaDescription: The archaeologist Alexander Ruttkay reflects on Svatopluk I, the role of Nitra in the 9th century and the meaning of that age for Slovak historical awareness.

keyFacts.label: Topic
keyFacts.value: Svatopluk I and his bond with Nitra in the light of written sources, archaeology and historical memory

keyFacts.label: Length of reign
keyFacts.value: more than 23 years – a third of the time Great Moravia lasted

keyFacts.label: Key sites
keyFacts.value: Nitra Castle, Devín, Bojná, Pobedim, Ducové, Nitrianska Blatnica

timeline.title: Foundation of the Nitra bishopric
timeline.description: The Nitra bishopric was established under Wiching, which documents the key ecclesiastical role of Nitra at the time of Svatopluk’s reign.

timeline.title: Frankish and Hungarian attack
timeline.description: The unsuccessful but devastating attack by the East Frankish king Arnulf and Hungarian cavalry called for large-scale fortification works at the hillforts, documented by dendrochronological analyses.

timeline.title: The death of Svatopluk
timeline.description: Svatopluk’s death ended a series of shifting alliances and decided the fate of a land that had lost a strong personality at its head.

timeline.title: The battle of Bratislava
timeline.description: Even after this battle, awareness persisted of the existence of more northerly, organisationally fragmented parts of the former Great Moravia.

timeline.title: Testimony of Hungarian captives near Córdoba
timeline.description: Hungarian warriors captured on the Iberian Peninsula testified that they had come from a territory bordering in the north on a country called Morabíja.

timeline.title: The Great Schism
timeline.description: After the church split into an eastern and a western branch, the history of the Kingdom of Hungary – and of the Sloveni within it – saw a turn towards Western Christianity.

timeline.title: The battle of Mohács
timeline.description: After this battle the Turkish author Mahmud Terdžümen described events connected with Svatopluk (Csopolug) from the time of the Hungarian conquest.

timeline.title: The 1,100th anniversary of Methodius’s death
timeline.description: On this occasion a large exhibition was held in the main pavilion of the Agrokomplex in Nitra and several synthesising publications on Great Moravia appeared.

timeline.title: The 1,100th anniversary of Svatopluk’s death
timeline.description: An interdisciplinary conference devoted to Svatopluk was held in Nitra; the papers delivered there were published in a separate edited volume.

children.text: With the kind permission of prof. PhDr. Alexander Ruttkay, DrSc., I am publishing his excellent article on Svatopluk and, more generally, his reflection on the history of the Slovaks and its significance for Slovak historical awareness. The article appeared in the pages of Literárny týždenník and also on the page of
the Klub priateľov starej Nitry (Club of Friends of Old Nitra), from where the article has been taken.

Historical anniversaries tied to events of the distant 9th century from time to time mobilise medievalists in Slovakia, stimulate scholarly research and publishing activity, and also inspire the creativity of artists.

In 1985, in connection with the 1,100th anniversary of Methodius’s death, a large representative exhibition was held in Nitra in the main pavilion of the Agrokomplex, and several synthesising publications also appeared. I shall mention two books in particular – Metodov boj (Methodius’s Struggle) by R. Marsina and Postavy veľkomoravskej histórie (Figures of Great Moravian History) by M. Kučera. In the second of these works the author attempted to sketch, in broader historical contexts yet deliberately and quite literally, even a sociological and psychological miniature portrait of Svatopluk I. Only in recollection does the name of Vojtech Matušinec still hover, together with his idea of building a new building for the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences on the hills in the western part of Nitra, and above it an equestrian statue of Svatopluk as much as 17 metres high. The master hoped for financial help from various sources, above all, it is said, from American Slovaks. He worked on the statue practically until his death (1992). V. Matušinec’s ideological starting points are reflected on the Facebook page called Slovenský stredovek (Slovak Middle Ages) in the presentation of the sculptor’s work, in words that I quote verbatim: “We must tell our nation the truth, cleanse our history of inventions and lies. No one else will do it for us. When the whole nation gains a true picture of the life and deeds of our ancestors, we shall be filled with admiration for the glory of ancient times. Yet the artist’s romantic notions and the technical possibilities of creating – and in the end also the need for – such a super-monumental equestrian statue were in deep contradiction, and it was not even possible to think seriously about its realisation.”

Time ran on, other ideas came, and the earlier ones seemed to be covered by oblivion. Yet in Nitra, on Zoborská kláštorná street, in the courtyard of V. Matušinec’s house, a huge sword and a horse’s head long reminded passers-by of the notion of a statue of Svatopluk in Nitra. With today’s technical possibilities it would perhaps be possible to work up a similar model on a computer as a 3-D presentation and use it in promoting the historical roots of the city beneath Zobor. I am no supporter of monumental statues. As a rule, statues should not stand high above their admirers. Life-size, they are better suited to a kind of direct, face-to-face communication with today’s world, especially in the setting of historical monuments, cultural institutions, parks and the like, where that proverbial spiritus loci – the spirit of the place – is also at work. Figures who, by their endurance in historical awareness at home and abroad and by their symbolic significance for present and future generations, deserve to stand in such places. From the earliest history of the territory of Slovakia these are above all Constantine and Methodius and, directly in relation to Nitra, especially Pribina, Svatopluk, Svorad and Benedict, Vazul, and let us not forget, for example, the important 11th-century duke of Nitra, Géza, called Magnus. Prince Pribina, portrayed long ago by T. Bártfay with a sword and what is probably a pilgrim’s bundle on his back, suggesting his spectacular departure from Nitra towards social advancement at the head of a principality in Pannonia, stands on “his” square and looks directly at visitors arriving in the Old Town and the castle. The sculptural group of the Thessalonian brothers by Ľ. Cvengrošová became, after the revolutionary changes of 1989 – despite initial protests from those whom any emphasis on figures connected with the history of the territory of Slovakia always and everywhere disturbs – a place where numerous visitors to Nitra Castle stop in reverence. There they see not only the presentation of archaeological excavations and restored architectural monuments, but also the important and long-awaited exhibition of the diocesan treasury.

A statue of Svatopluk, however, is missing in Nitra, and this despite the hymn-like song recorded by Ján Kollár in his Spievanky as early as the first half of the 19th century. The well-known Nitra, milá Nitra (Nitra, dear Nitra) is probably a tangible reference, resting on far older traditions, to the historical bond between our city and the prince of Nitra and ruler of Great Moravia. In the centre of Nitra there is Svätoplukovo námestie (Svatopluk Square); perhaps there the will and the place could be found for a statue of the figure who, among the secular protagonists of Great Moravia, is the only one to have remained continuously in Central European historical awareness. In 1994, on the occasion of the 1,100th anniversary of Svatopluk’s death, an interdisciplinary conference was held in Nitra. The papers delivered there were published in a separate edited volume. I have now leafed through this volume again after many years, revived in myself the euphoria that followed the founding of the Slovak Republic, and compared it in the spectrum of today’s broader and more sober view of things long past as well, and not only of present ones. Of those concrete, verified facts relating directly to the person of Svatopluk, practically none have been added over the last ten years. Only the archaeological evidence, which I shall mention in the next part of this reflection, has brought new insights into the organisation of the defence of the territory of the eastern parts of the core of Great Moravia at the end of Svatopluk’s life. There is no room here for possible “innovations” or interpretative variations of the “what if” type; these should be left to inventive journalists with a greater willingness to unfold their imaginative powers…

Svatopluk, wrapped in myths and legends over the advancing centuries, symbolises the need for unity and concord of the whole community as a precondition of success in all areas of life. The legendary three twigs are the central idea of Eugen Suchoň’s opera Svätopluk. It corresponds to the symbolism of the ruler’s figure and his relationship to Nitra that this great operatic work was performed by the opera of the Slovak National Theatre directly beneath Nitra Castle. It was the opening of the series of annual concerts Hoj, vlasť moja… (Hail, my homeland…), which continue to this day thanks above all to the steady initiative of L. Švihel, the long-serving director of the Agrokomplex enterprise, and to the dedication of numerous artists and organisers. The idea that Svatopluk resided in Nitra and should have a memorial here was briefly revived in 2010 by the discussion about the siting of the equestrian statue of Svatopluk. This was reflected in several offers to take over the statue of Svatopluk from Bratislava. The ruler of Great Moravia, a man whose name was not dragged out of the twilight of oblivion in the age of the national revival of the peoples of Central Europe but lived on continuously through long centuries, with recognition of its bearer’s intellectual and military-political abilities, in the German, Czech and Hungarian milieus, deserves a statue in the capital of the Slovak Republic, for instance with the titulature “prince of Nitra and ruler of Great Moravia”. Bratislava Castle developed continuously on the site of a Great Moravian hillfort which, on the basis of insights from earlier archaeological excavations led by T. Štefanovičová, also had an important power-related and ecclesiastical function in Svatopluk’s time. Leaving aside the short-lived “temporariness” of the political disputes surrounding this statue, which will certainly gradually subside, from a rigorous scholarly point of view objections could be raised to iconographic details of the statue (conspicuous, for example, are the spurs with rowels, which are typical only from the 13th century onwards, or the sheet-metal parts of the armour belonging to the High Middle Ages). Yet here too the licence of the creative artist – the author of the work – and his vision of the timeless symbolism of a historical figure applies. What is more, the sculptural depiction of important persons does not fully correspond to authentic period reality in other cases either. I shall mention the well-known equestrian statues of Prince St Stephen. It would never occur to me, however, when judging works of art, to put “scientific” analyses in the foreground. An artistic rendering is not a period reconstruction. The model for an artistic vision of Svatopluk is therefore not the appearance of a 9th-century Great Moravian warrior on horseback. In the case of the statue of Svatopluk, J. Kulich set himself a demanding artistic goal and achieved it: to depict a rider on a steed rearing after a sudden pull of the bit. Such a depiction, which is perhaps similar to the one in V. Matušinec’s imaginative design, is among the most demanding artistic forms of equestrian statue. One can place side by side – at least in a picture – the statue of Svatopluk and the miniature model of Leonardo da Vinci’s equestrian statue. The great Leonardo reworked his anatomically and kinetically masterly work many times, yet in the end it was never cast in bronze at life size, despite the efforts of the French king Francis I – the last patron of that brilliant artist.

During the dispute over the statue in Bratislava, Svatopluk as a person was often relished even by citizens who have no knowledge whatever of the complex problems of the history and culture of the Early Middle Ages. In one discussion, for example, I came across the “opinion” of one of the rank-and-file representatives of the media that an equestrian statue will not stand up because in that period the Slavs had no cavalry. Behind the critical emphasis on the unsuitability of the author of the Svatopluk statue at Bratislava Castle, on his titulature (king, prince, ruler), on the “political” conditions of the statue’s erection and so on, however, the cornerstone of the negation is, besides personal rivalry among artists, also naive posturing, or perhaps somewhere still deeper a negation of the identity of Slovakia and of the historical figures who, regardless of their ethnic origin, are connected with its territory. Figures from the 14th century come to mind – Matúš Čák, Magister the Knight Donč, Vavrinec Slavus (Tóth – the Slovak), owner of Tematín Castle and founder of the well-known family of the lords of Ilok (Ujlaki); from the 15th to 17th centuries – Ján Korvín of Liptov, Ján and Rafael Podmanický of Považská Bystrica, Valentín Balaša of Zvolen or Imrich Tököli of Kežmarok, and so on. Against each of them – how else – a mass of objections would appear. Just look at how even a Jánošík was suddenly degraded here and there in some media from his symbolic post to an almost run-of-the-mill brigand. Resistance to historical figures directly related to the territory of Slovakia is rooted above all within this society, in the negation of the past and, after 1993, also in the questioning of the prospects of “this country”. But as the saying goes, “that too will yield in time”.

Such associations, and many others, should be noted in the contexts of the history of Slovakia. It is a challenge for the historical sciences to study not only the ethnic history of the nation but the history of civilisational development in the territory of Slovakia within several pre-Great Moravian principalities, the Principality of Nitra, Great Moravia and medieval Hungary. The continuity of Slavic occupation – and hence also the genetic code and above all the continuity in the development of the language – is clearly documented from the 5th–6th centuries. As regards the ethnic name, before the 9th century the general designation Slavs (Slovania) is probably appropriate, in the 9th–13th centuries Sloveni, and from the 14th century Slovaks (Slováci). The remark in one weekly that Slovak archaeologists have not yet found a single “old Slovak” is not only naive and demagogic but downright comic. The number of unfortified and fortified settlements and cemeteries of the 8th–9th centuries that belong to the local population, the ancestors of today’s Slovak nation, currently amounts to more than 800 sites. There is no question here of the name “Slovak”, still less of some ethnic “purity of blood”. There can be no question of a phenomenon of national purity in the case of any present-day European nation. In the genesis of the Sloveni in the Great Moravian period, from the 5th–6th centuries onwards, besides the influx of Slavic population from the northern – Sclavene – current, there was probably also present a not very numerous local ethnic substrate from the remnants of Germanic and perhaps, in origin, also Celtic populations, possibly also Slavicised Avars and the like. And in the development of Slovak nationality in the Middle Ages the decisive element is the continuity of occupation from pre-Hungarian times and, later, its capacity to assimilate several smaller – Slavic and other – ethnic groups which settled in the Slovak milieu in various periods. If the idea of such a “mixing” of ethnic groups should seem to someone a disappointment, or even a “heresy”, then a similar multigenetic process with several links took place in past centuries and is, after all, taking place today as well – practically in the milieu of all European nations, including our closest neighbours. For in the development of ethnic identity it is language and territory, that is, the concept of homeland, that are decisive, while cultural and historical awareness and also fixed names of ethnic groups – of nations in today’s sense of the word – were formed gradually only later. From the point of view of the social structure of medieval Hungary, what stood in the foreground was not ethnic but social division. The decisive factor was the supra-ethnic category of the stratum of feudal lords and the deep differences between social groups. Yet if we were to judge ethnic categorisation – which is only a virtual view – by present-day criteria, then the population with Slovak as its mother tongue had a structure that included higher, middle and lower nobility, clergy at all levels, a smaller share among townspeople, and popular strata with various forms of livelihood. The significance of the languages of all medieval ethnic groups in Hungary was overlaid by universal Latin.

Let us return, however, to the topic of Svatopluk I. In assessments of him there are frequent attempts to weigh above all ethical principles in connection with his relations to Rastislav and then to Methodius and his disciples. Often only partial aspects stand in the foreground, and not the broader historical and geographical context. Thus it could happen that Svatopluk is even considered, in part of both the scholarly and the artistic imagination, a traitor in relation to Rastislav and the liquidator of the Cyrillo-Methodian mission. Yet details about events, and especially about interpersonal interactions in distant centuries, are most often impossible to reconstruct. It is no different in the case of events that took place much later. All that remains at our disposal is a reflection of the real deeds; their positive and negative values will then be judged by the future. Svatopluk’s period may be compared, for example, with events a hundred years later at the beginnings of the Hungarian state – there too it was a struggle for power with no scruples about the means, and there too, in connection with the acceptance of Christianity, both an eastern, Byzantine, and a western, Roman orientation were at first in play. Especially after the schism of 1054, the advantages of the turn towards the western branch of Christianity became apparent in the history of the Kingdom of Hungary – and of the Sloveni within it. Svatopluk’s period, with its dynamism and its great social, political and territorial changes, represents the peak of the historical development of the oldest state of the Western Slavs and at the same time the beginnings of its deep internal crisis. It was a period that contradicts traditional notions about the undeveloped state of warfare among the Slavs. The reality was entirely different. The strategy and tactics of combat, the quality of the weapons, and also the cruelty with which wars were waged – yes, including Svatopluk’s expansive campaigns of conquest – were within the norm of the Europe of that time. Objective facts about this were discovered above all by archaeology. At the same time it has provided partial arguments for the lasting position of this ancient and powerful ruler in historical awareness. The connection of Svatopluk with Nitra was preserved by medieval literary sources. Besides the well-known passage in the Czech chronicle of Cosmas from the beginning of the 12th century, I shall recall at least two less frequently cited sources which have at the very least the character of ancient traditions. The Kremsmünster notes on the bishops of Passau, compiled at the turn of the 13th and 14th centuries, state that Bishop Wiching wanted to divide the Lorch diocese and create his own archbishopric with the help of King svätopluk in Sclavia (hic!) – this is undoubtedly Nitra. Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, from 1458 Pope Pius II, states in his treatise published in Rome in 1475 that Svatopluk died in the monastery on Zobor. To these sources I shall add two further little-known pieces of information from the 16th century, which prove that the name of Svatopluk was alive and is even a kind of personification of the Slavs in the Middle Danube region before the arrival of the Hungarians. The Turkish author Mahmud Terdžümen, in a work on the history of Hungary written only after the fateful battle of Mohács (1526), says of the events after the arrival of the Hungarian tribes that they attacked Svatopluk (Csopolug) from Transylvania and that after his defeat they supposedly moved against Pest. This is an error: at the time of the Hungarian conquest Svatopluk was already dead. According to another 16th-century work entitled Commentarii rebus de suo tempore (Notes on the History of the Present) by Ludovicus Tubero, the Hungarian tribes wedged themselves between the southern and the northern Slavs and thereby separated them from one another.

Historical works from the 18th century onwards had at their disposal, in the decisive majority, the written sources on the 9th century that are used and interpreted today. Until then, new elements had evidently emerged only in the Vatican archives. The name Great Moravia, which is not identical with the designation of the later historical Moravia, and the emphasis on Nitra as Svatopluk’s seat belonged among the generally accepted facts in older historically oriented writing. In connection with the history of Nitra and of the Nitra bishopric, the book of the Nitra bishop Jozef Vurum of 1835 deserves particular attention. Some of the data and opinions in the work are captive to the level of historical views of the time and cannot be accepted (for example about a bishopric in Nitra at the end of the 4th century). Most of the data it presents, however, are historical realities. The passage on Nitra as Pribina’s seat, the outline of the history of the Slavs north of the Danube in the 9th century, the deeds of Mojmír, Rastislav and Svatopluk, the characterisation of the magnificent activity of Cyril and Methodius, and the founding of the Nitra diocese in 880 under Wiching – all this indicates that the written sources on the history of Great Moravia (J. Vurum unambiguously uses the term Magnae Moraviae Regnum – that is, a kingdom) were subjected to a framework historical analysis from which the important role of Nitra emerged, including the old tradition about Svatopluk’s seat. Such an interpretation is also the basis of the monograph on Nitra County from the end of the 19th century. It pays attention to Svatopluk, who resided in Nitra and was said to be among the most capable Slavic political and military figures of the Early Middle Ages. His death and the subsequent weakening of the “empire” facilitated the victorious Hungarian military advance. From all these literary sources the key role of Nitra in the pre-Hungarian period emerges, including the tradition about one of Svatopluk’s main seats. If that is so, then on the basis of the results of many years of excavation at Nitra Castle it can be stated that a 9th-century hillfort with an area of almost 9 hectares stood on this spot, that there was evidently a church here already before the 10th century, and that it was precisely in the second half of the 9th century that the massive fortification was renewed here. This is not, admittedly, anything like “exact proof” of Svatopluk’s seat, but it testifies to the paramount importance of Nitra during his reign. On the castle hill, following the excavations led by P. Bednár, one more remarkable discovery is taking shape. In the massive fortification, probably connected with the period of Svatopluk’s reign, decorative architectural elements originating from an older building, already dismantled by that time, were re-used. Is this perhaps material from the famous little church of Pribina, which may have perished after Mojmír’s expansion and was replaced during Svatopluk’s reign by a church already dedicated to St Emmeram? Another indication – which again is connected with Svatopluk’s tactical procedures in matters of relations with the church – is the emergence of the Nitra bishopric under Wiching. Among the reflections of this more frequently westward-turned view of Svatopluk are probably also the Frankish dedications: alongside St Emmeram on the castle hill there is also St Hyplit for the monastery on Zobor, with beginnings in the time of Wiching’s activity here and connected probably also with the activities of the monastery of St Hippolytus in St Pölten. The reputed activity of the Old Slovak school in Nitra might, under favourable circumstances, also be served by archaeological excavation of the Zobor monastery, which did indeed begin in recent years with promising results (it was led by M. Samuel) but is not continuing for the time being. In older Hungarian historical research, the main sources on the progress of the conquest of older centres of power in the territory of Slovakia in the 10th century included the chronicle of the so-called Anonymus from the end of the 12th century. Its data cannot be accepted as facts, but some of them need to be “decoded” in a certain way in space and time, since at the time the chronicle was written they seemed credible to contemporaries. The chronicle is tendentious and consists of numerous confabulations, but it also dimly and distortedly reflects some events of the 10th–11th centuries and even from before 896. The chronicler certainly knew, and does not deny, that north of the core of the territory of the Hungarian state there was, before the arrival of the ancestors of the Hungarians, a strong Slavic power formation, that is, Great Moravia, and that several of its centres were located in the territory of Slovakia. After the conquest of evidently the most important one, the action of three mythical (?) leaders supposedly led to the Váh region (there is no mention of an advance in the Nitra or Hron regions!), where they were to seize the castles of Šintava, Hlohovec, Bana, Beckov and Trenčín. Awareness of the existence of more northerly, organisationally probably fragmented parts of the former Great Moravia even after the battle of Bratislava in 907 is suggested by the testimony of Hungarian warriors captured in 942 in the territory of the Caliphate of Córdoba on the Iberian Peninsula during their military expedition. They had come from a territory which supposedly borders in the north on a country called Morabíja. In older Hungarian historical awareness, a strong Slovak power in the more southerly parts of Slovakia before the Hungarian conquest was taken for granted. This territory was not designated as a marginal part of Great Moravia. For example, in 1828 A. Mednyánszky included not only Nitra but also the five other castles mentioned among the originally Great Moravian fortresses conquered by Hungarian warriors. In 1912, after his ascent to the now famous hillfort of Valy above Bojná, I. Némethy emphasised the great strength of the Slavic “element” in the country before the Hungarian military occupation. I shall also mention the opinion of the well-known writer K. Mikszáth, who in his stories about the “knightly castles of Hungary” (1907) included Nitra, Hlohovec and Visegrád as well. According to him, the Hungarians found these already finished; they had originally had them built and Slovak (tót) princes resided in them. The site of Višegrád was supposedly named by Slovak lords and not by serfs, as people had by then (the writer himself emphasised this) “begun to say in Pest circles”. The Vyšehrad belonging to the 9th century was the hillfort, still visible today, with a ruined church on the hill of Šibirik. K. Mikszáth uses the older Hungarian ethnic term “tót” (that is, before the 14th century, Sloven) – without the familiar pejorative context that was formed later – and not the general designation szláv (Slav). Here one can perhaps see the now little-known, essentially realistic world of views held by part of the Hungarian intelligentsia in the 19th century about the local organisation of society and power before the arrival of the Hungarians. I shall now attempt, on the basis of new, above all archaeological sources, to sketch in outline my view of the relationship of legends, traditions, myths and mythology to historical facts, to look at Svatopluk as a personality “making history” and also as a “pillar” of historical awareness. This concerns a period of “heroes” and of a distinctive warrior morality, honour and generosity, of contacts between paganism and Christianity, as reflected in the epic works of those European regions where such works have survived from the Early Middle Ages. Fragments of the legends and heroic songs of the Slavs north of the Danube are perhaps reflected in the medieval Hungarian chronicles as well…

Even though Svatopluk’s relationship to Nitra is expressed as if “only” in legends and, from the beginning of the 1st century, also in narrative written sources, the real historical background of such ancient messages cannot be underestimated. They reflect something of ancient events that are at present scientifically unknowable, or at least of their indirect echo in the awareness of descendants. I am not inclined to change the symbolism of ancient events anchored in national awareness, as it is among other nations as well; I respect, and with reverence for their antiquity I bow before, the many legends and traditions emerging from the mists of the distant past. The mythologisation of these messages is natural too; they are an inseparable part of creative work in various artistic genres and have thus become practically “opinion-forming”. Slovakia is no exception in this respect. The historical awareness of many European nations rests partly on myths fixed by long-term educational influence as a kind of “historical reality”, the substance and strategic aims of which were not changed by changes of regime, of political circumstances and the like. A legend sometimes becomes a legitimate source of inspiration and comparison even from the point of view of scholarly enquiry. Yet the colourful local colour of ancient and recent traditions and legends, living or in the making – in modern parlance almost like “titbits” and “causes célèbres” – should not tempt the historian or the archaeologist onto easier paths; they must not replace historical interpretation. This applies to the 9th century just as much as to the 20th and the 21st.

Scholarly knowledge must, however, inevitably cross the barrier created by fixed traditions. The history of the Moravians and the Sloveni of the 9th century appears today differently from how it was known and believed until recently. The quality of the insights for modelling the beginnings of state-forming processes in the territory of present-day Slovakia has changed. Thanks to new discoveries, especially in the more mountainous areas of western and central Slovakia, traditional views of socio-organisational and state-building development have changed surprisingly, especially for the period before that firm point which is the well-known conflict between Pribina and Mojmír. The middle Váh region, the middle and upper Nitra region, the Žilina Basin, Turiec, lower Liptov with the adjacent part of Orava, Spiš and probably also the Zvolen Basin – these are regions outside the direct power sphere of the Avar Khaganate already in the 8th century. Already after 800, hillforts – fortified organisational centres and seats of territorial princes – were being established here. Together with the ancient centres in Nitra and at Devín, an ecumene emerges in which, under circumstances not known in detail, the Principality of Nitra acquired the dominant role. It was probably an ally of the Frankish Empire in the destruction of the Avar Khaganate at the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries and soon built up positions of power on the northern bank of the Danube as well. The union of the two principalities – the Nitra one (originally with its axis on the river Nitra and between the White Carpathians and the Hron) and the Moravian one (originally with its axis on the river Orava, with a sphere of influence as far as the Lesser and the White Carpathians, or possibly as far as the Váh) – appears as the conclusion of a longer-running process of integration. Pribina, prince of Nitra and later of Pannonia, with the circle of magnates who accompanied him after his departure from Nitra, was not alone; his predecessors, unknown to us by name, or also his contemporaries and possibly rivals in the struggle for power, left clear traces behind them. The famous, long-known and seemingly isolated magnate graves from Blatnica or Žabokreky in Turiec have been placed in the contexts of the present state of knowledge. They belong to representatives of a ruling stratum which, in an environment that already before the 9th century shows a tendency towards growth of occupation, built fortified seats, several of which have already been identified in the field. Some of the hillforts perished probably as early as around the middle of the 9th century (for example Pobedim – excavation by D. Bialeková) as a result of unification processes, that is, in connection with the emergence of Great Moravia, or they went through a temporary decline. The composition of the material culture is characteristic of the pre-Great Moravian phase of their existence. The artistic craft products represent the so-called Blatnica style; the armament already in this period inclines towards western – especially Frankish – forms. The dominant figure became the horseman with sword and spurs, while the infantry, armed chiefly with axes and spears, represents older local Slavic traditions. The first evidence connected with pre-Cyrillo-Methodian Christianisation activities, perhaps already of Irish-Scottish but above all of northern Italian (Aquileia) and Frankish origin, also appears in this region. Some of these hillforts remained nodes of power in the Great Moravian period as well (for example Bojná – the ongoing excavation is led by K. Pieta), those lying further north (for example Pružiná) continuously also in the post-Great Moravian period, and others – especially Nitra (numerous excavations from 1958 to 199 under the direction of B. Chropovský), Bratislava and Devín (excavation by V. Plachá) – retained a leading position in the period of the Hungarian state. In the second half of the 9th century new hillforts arose, for example Sv. Jur, probably also Mužla-Čenkov and Bíňa, Majcichov (excavation by M. Ruttkay) and Detva (excavation by P. Šalkovský). Some hillforts in the area of the Slovenská brána (the Slovak Gate), for example Malé Kozmálovce, Krivín and Hronský Beňadik (excavation by A. Habovštiak), may have barred entry from the south into the more mountainous parts of the Hron region in the 10th century. Unfortunately, until recently evidence of writing from the 9th century, or from an earlier period, that originated directly in the territory of Slovakia or Moravia was lacking. In the recent period this situation has changed, if only slightly: several letters – Latin ones – have appeared on the precious plaques from a portable altar at Bojná, from the period before the arrival of Constantine and Methodius. Their origin and significance are being analysed. Fragments of the Cyrillo-Methodian Glagolitic script, however, have most recently been found only on pottery from the extensive excavation of the seat of Pribina and Koceľ by Lake Balaton (currently led by B. Szöke). I believe, however, that the parts of the inscription from Michalovce associated with the Bulgarian Presian of the 11th century probably do not belong among such sources. It could rather be an inscription in Cyrillic from the 16th–17th centuries. I want to recall certain long-known inscriptions on rocks which are a priori regarded as forgeries and were therefore entirely excluded from the process of enquiry in any possible reconnaissance. For example Velestúr in the mountains near Kremnica has been known for a century and a half and still belongs among the monuments visible to this day. I use the term monument without the usual quotation marks, since by its age the inscription belongs at the very least deep into the 19th century. It might be worth subjecting it to objective verification analyses using modern technology to see whether it really originated only in the 19th century. Even if it did, it represents a remarkable element in the history of the national revival that would deserve a certain attention, protection and promotion. And this applies to other mysterious guaranteed “forgeries” as well. In archaeology, too, it has happened that out of several guaranteed insignificant, or even supposedly “invented”, find spots there gradually emerged sites of paramount importance. And there are of course cases to the contrary. It is always important, however, to verify opinions and conjectures.

It is possible that all the regions mentioned in the more mountainous parts of Slovakia did not become a direct part of Great Moravia immediately after the departure of Pribina and his retinue from Nitra. The takeover was a gradual process and may have continued under the reign of Rastislav and especially under Svatopluk. It was precisely during his campaigns that the sphere of the “empire” evidently shifted as far as the Tisza, into the neighbourhood of the Bulgarian power sphere of the time. Svatopluk’s devastating raids into Pannonia may also have rested on a more firmly occupied forefield in the area of the Piliš hills with the hillfort of Vyšehrad (Visegrád). Two remarkable phenomena have also been established archaeologically in Slovakia, in which the social development of the second half of the 9th century, and indeed of the last years of Svatopluk’s life, is reflected. The ruler’s military strength rested above all on cavalry, on the members of the so-called senior and junior retinue. The very frequent occurrence of spurs, stirrups, horse bits and other parts of riding equipment, often employing complex production and decorative techniques, testifies to the great role of cavalry in the Great Moravian period. The problem of feeding a growing number of professional armed men who already belonged to the social elite, and their role – if need required – of applying repression against the ordinary population alongside their combat duties, called for the territorial dislocation of part of the mounted retinue. Alongside the central nodes, external magnate domains arose. Their strength grew especially in the period of Svatopluk I; among the seats of magnates the manorial-court type probably predominated (excavations by the author of this contribution), whether with a military-administrative (Ducové) or an economic (Nitrianska Blatnica) function. Further smaller armed groups came into being at the private manorial courts. This is a new element – a military retinue maintained by a magnate but which, from the military point of view, was part of the princely armies when needed. In critical situations a decentralising aspect could manifest itself, supporting the power-related and separatist aspirations of individual members of the new aristocracy. Frankish sources mostly inform us only superficially about the defence of Great Moravia during the frequent Frankish incursions. New results have been obtained thanks to dendrochronological analyses of material from the fortifications of some hillforts. Large-scale fortification works were carried out, for example, probably at the time of the devastating but ultimately not entirely successful attack of the East Frankish king Arnulf and Hungarian cavalry in 892–893. Alliances changed quickly, however – immediately afterwards came Svatopluk’s offensive in alliance with the Hungarians against Arnulf. The further course of these shifting alliances was ended in 894 by Svatopluk’s death. The fate of the land he ruled, and which had lost a strong personality at its head, was decided.

In conclusion I shall return once more to Svatopluk through the eyes of today’s citizen, who inevitably sees certain analogies in history and sometimes, purposefully or subconsciously, brings them up to date. In what do I see Svatopluk’s position in the age in which he lived? His military qualities are emphasised; he did, after all, pursue an expansive policy from the point of view of Great Moravia, he seized large territories mostly for a shorter time, he led devastating expeditions into Pannonia, and with his name is associated a stage of the “empire” of the Western Slavs. Less prominent are his diplomatic abilities, his successful strategic and tactical thinking and, for instance, the building of fortress installations – extremely demanding on the organisation of the population – against the growing Frankish and Hungarian threat at the end of his life. The more than twenty-three-year period of Svatopluk’s reign represents a third of the time Great Moravia lasted and, with its great social, political and territorial changes – including, for example, the beginnings of social relations that we may already describe as proto-feudal – it represents the peak of historical development in the territory of Slovakia in the 9th century as well. The special function of Nitra – especially on the basis of more recent archaeological discoveries on the castle hill – is indisputable. It belonged among the so-called castle towns of Great Moravia, it was one of the ruler’s seats with a network of surrounding production and farming settlements, a core of advancing Christianisation and a node of long-distance trade. After the demise of Great Moravia, too, it became, until the beginning of the 12th century, the seat of the early Hungarian duchy. Svatopluk was a man who could evidently have great aims; in pursuing them – like other historical protagonists – he was not choosy about the means, but he was not defeated… His pragmatic turn to the west, his purposeful diplomatic manoeuvring – which we know, for example, from his ambivalent steps in the relationship between Methodius and the penetrating Frankish clergy – speak to us too, to people of the present, and sometimes literally serve as a warning. Christianity, early forms of feudal relations, the level of craft production and above all the lifestyle of the social elite are comparable above all with the East Frankish milieu. The later phase of expansion, the military successes, the maximum extension of at least temporarily controlled territories, meant a growth of power, bringing Svatopluk’s domain closer to the content of the concept of an “empire”, with smouldering elements of instability. They foreshadow the prospect of fragmentation, disintegration, gradual demise, or military subjugation from the south and from the west. Causes, deeds and consequences – that is the eternal, literally “Hamletian” dilemma of historical processes… These final phases of development, however, took place only after Svatopluk’s death; neither historical facts nor traditions connect him with the demise of the centrally governed Great Moravian principality.

The history of the territory of Slovakia needs, more than has hitherto been customary, to be “peopled” with real personalities who should resonate in the awareness of descendants as protagonists creating, through their work and through the complex twists of history, a path to the present.

prof. PhDr. Alexander Ruttkay, DrSc.
